action_plan.task: /brainstorm then rebalance the rat variants: what each rat is FOR, given that damage cannot be a trade-off in this game
action_plan.done_when: Across a spread of levels the two variants clear in comparable hit counts, or heavy pays a cost that shows up in the score - measured, not assumed
action_plan.context: Measured 2026-09-12 from human play on the rope build. Heavy carries impactMultiplier 2.2 and mass 11.5 against standard 1.0 and 4.5, and swings only ~15% slower (calibration p50 113 vs 134). Since damage goes as speed squared, heavy nets 2.2 x (113/134)^2 = 1.56x effective damage - slower does not come close to paying for the multiplier. Observed: heavy median 3 hits vs standard 6, and because score is max(200, 3000-(hits-1)*500) that compounds into 1000-2500 vs 500. The lever is impactMultiplier, NOT DAMAGE_SCALE, which divides both variants equally. Needs the design gate: making heavy weaker, slower, or giving standard something of its own are different games. STRENGTHENED 2026-09-12 by L1 data, which invalidates the trade-off premise entirely: in actual play both variants swing at the SAME speed (p50 114.4 standard vs 114.1 heavy). The earlier -15% figure came from free-swing calibration and does not survive contact with real play, so heavy pays NO speed cost for its 2.2x multiplier. Observed damage per hit 18.3 vs 7.7 = 2.4x, matching the multiplier with nothing offsetting it. Heavy also lands cleaner (15% glancing vs 31%), plausibly because its radius is 22 against 18. Heavy is better on every measured axis: same speed, 2.4x damage, cleaner hits, bigger body. There is no trade-off to balance - the variant is simply strictly better. SCOPE SET 2026-09-12: user chose a full design gate over a quick constant change. THE STRUCTURAL PROBLEM the design must solve: the goal is to destroy YOUR OWN rat in as few hits as possible and score is max(200, 3000-(hits-1)*500), so taking more damage per hit is purely good - there is no downside to trade against, and any variant with a higher multiplier is permanently strictly better. The usual counterweight is unavailable too: heavy mass 11.5 should swing slower, but the player drives the pivot directly so the hand overrides mass, which is why both variants clock identical in-play speed (114.1 vs 114.4). Mass-based trade-offs do not survive this control scheme. Options sketched and NOT chosen: cut heavy impactMultiplier 2.2 -> ~1.25; equalise damage and differentiate on feel/blast/appearance; keep heavy strong but apply a score penalty. Also note the arithmetic trap: standard needs ~3.3x damage to reach 4 hits on L1, which would drop heavy to ~1.4 hits, so DAMAGE_SCALE cannot move until this resolves. DESIGN GATE CLOSED 2026-09-13: chose the difficulty-selector framing with par-relative scoring - see the 2026-09-13 decisions entry. Implementation is tasks 130-133; 126 closes when task 133 measures the predicted hit counts, since its done_when demands measured, not assumed. MEASUREMENT 2026-09-13 PARTLY REFUTES THE DESIGN. Solved: heavy is no longer strictly better on damage, and the hit-count gap collapsed from 2.10x (10.5 vs 5.0) to 1.13x (3.4 vs 3.0). NOT solved, and INVERTED: standard now out-scores heavy by 800 on average (3800 vs 3000), so standard is the dominant pick. Cause is parHits, exactly the lever flagged in advance, though the direction was predicted wrong: standard was predicted at 5.2 hits and given par 5, but plays at 3.4, so it beats its par by 1.6 hits every run for a free +800, while heavy's par 3 matches its measured 3.0 exactly. DEEPER FINDING: the difficulty-selector premise did not survive measurement at all. Both variants now play in a 2-4 hit band with means 3.4 and 3.0, which is indistinguishable at n=5, and the precision axis (31% vs 15% glancing) that the whole design rested on does not translate into a hit-count difference at this damage scale. A 3-4 hit target simply leaves no room to express variant difference - there is nowhere in a 2-4 band to put a gap. PAR CORRECTED 2026-09-13: standard 5 -> 4, its measured median, cutting the residual advantage from +800 to +300 which is inside the noise at n=5. The framing question is deferred to task 143.

(1) The tail was not drawn at all in READY, because showTail required a stringConstraint - exactly what the pick-up has not created yet - and drawTail prepended the stale level pivot as a control point. (2) SCREENSHOT CAUGHT WHAT THE GATE COULD NOT: the tail settled into a coil within a second, since pairwise constraints hold neighbours 13px apart but nothing keeps the chain straight. That made the tip position non-deterministic and broke the plan for task 142. Fixed with Physics.freezeForGrab, holding the pose static until the grab; the rendered tip then matched the predicted 350.5 exactly.

decisions.decision: Remove fling mode entirely — delete RELEASED state, fling input handling, and mode picker UI

decisions.decision: Redesign levels as 9 levels in 3 acts (Sewer/Warehouse/Lab); Act 2 introduces destructible shields; Act 3 introduces bumpers; act-grouped level select with ACT CLEAR screen
decisions.rationale: Levels felt samey with no new mechanics; acts provide structure and escalation; shields/bumpers implementable with existing physics primitives

decisions.decision: Items 35+36 combined: PointerEvents API in input.js + CSS transform scaling via fitToViewport() in main.js
decisions.rationale: Single codepath for mouse and touch; getBoundingClientRect in getCanvasXY automatically compensates for CSS scale transform, so no coordinate math changes needed anywhere

decisions.decision: Damage formula: speed² × angleFactor × material.yoyoDamage × impactMultiplier × comboMultiplier / DAMAGE_SCALE (1200), replacing linear speed/15
decisions.rationale: Speed-squared creates a meaningful skill ceiling: 1-hit possible at max speed (~450 px/step), 3 hits at good play (~250 px/step), casual players take 5-9 hits. Glass/wood shield breakSpeeds lowered from 140/300 to 100/180 — wood shield at 300 was unreachable. DAMAGE_SCALE is a single named constant for easy post-play tuning.

decisions.decision: Migrated project management files (spec.md, CLAUDE.md, project-state.json, .gitignore, TEST_SPEC.md) to the frameworklite scaffold, preserving existing git history and game code as-is — no game files moved or renamed
decisions.rationale: Project was feature-complete (43/43 prior action items done); frameworklite's session-briefing/action-plan conventions add continuity without disrupting the working game or its commit history on origin/main

decisions.decision: Tail-attachment redesign (combined #46+#47): move the rat's swing constraint from its center to a tail-base anchor point, paired with mass/frictionAir tuning on both variants; the rope visual (drawString) is replaced by the rat's own tail stretching to the pivot, and rotation switches from accumulated spinAngle to physics-driven body.angle
decisions.rationale: An off-center attachment lets gravity naturally torque the rat to hang below the grip point — literally 'held by the tail' — while also being the most direct, lowest-risk lever for the weightless feel (#47), since it doesn't touch collision detection, fragment spawning, or the damage formula. A two-body ragdoll rat was considered and rejected as architecturally oversized for this scope.

decisions.decision: Tail-attachment rebalance settled after 4 rounds of playtesting. Final values — standard rat: mass 1.0→4.5, frictionAir 0.005→0.025, restitution 0.35→0.05; heavy rat: mass 3.5→11.5, frictionAir 0.003→0.015, restitution 0.1→0.02; constraint stiffness 0.65→0.35
decisions.rationale: The first two tuning passes (mass/frictionAir increases, stiffness decreases) weren't enough — user reported no major difference. The decisive change was reversing frictionAir direction to a sharp ~5x increase (faster momentum decay, more effort to reach top speed) and dropping rat restitution near zero (less bounce, more hit-and-slide). Accepted as good for now. Caveat: Matter.js resolves collision restitution as max(rat, target), so steel targets (restitution 0.55 in target.js) will still bounce regardless of the rat's value — a target.js follow-up if that surfaces during task 45's full playthrough.

decisions.decision: Heavier impact feedback (supersedes #48, expanded to include rat body-wear): extend particles.js with a rotating 'chunk' shape; on every HP-damage hit, fire three damage-scaled bursts (red blood splash, target-material chunk debris via material.crackedColor, rat-fur chunk debris via a new variant color); reuse the already-generated-but-unrendered yoyo.plugin.crackPattern to draw scuff marks on the rat's body via drawCracks(), plus an HP-based body color blend toward a new worn tone
decisions.rationale: Builds entirely on existing systems — particles.js's emit/update/draw loop, target.js's crackedColor palette, and main.js's dormant per-hit crackPattern generation for the rat body — so no new physics bodies or rendering pipelines are needed. This keeps the change low-risk and avoids the perf cost of spawning Matter.js fragments on every combo hit (a physics-debris approach was considered and rejected for that reason). The new 'chunk' particle shape gives debris a distinct angular silhouette from the round blood splashes.

decisions.decision: Heavier impact feedback rebalanced after playtesting: chunk/debris particle radius now scales from 1x (current size, at damageIntensity 0) up to 3x (at damageIntensity 1) instead of a fixed size; chunk-shaped particles also have an 8% chance to spawn 2.5x-4x oversized for rare visual variety; SHATTER-time giblet fragments render as one of 4 random shapes (blob/triangle/rect/diamond) instead of always ellipses
decisions.rationale: First playtesting pass found the fixed debris size didn't read as more impactful on harder hits, and the uniform ellipse giblets looked repetitive on shatter. Scaling radius with damageIntensity (already used for particle count) ties debris size directly to hit strength with no new state; the 8% oversized roll and shapeType variety (physics.js fragment plugin field, consumed in renderer.js drawFragments) add visual variance cheaply since both reuse existing per-particle/per-fragment data.

decisions.decision: Four-part tuning/feature round (tasks 63-74), surfaced during task 45's playthrough: (1) recalibrate speed meter + damage formula — pushMaxSpeed ×1.25 (standard 600→750, heavy 500→625) and DAMAGE_SCALE 1200→2000, with the shake-threshold and damageIntensity-saturation constants rescaled ×0.6 to match — so the realistic top swing speed reads as 60% on the meter and 1-hit shatters require near-max effort/combo; (2) shape variety — convert 3 rectangle targets (levels 1, 3, 7) to circles; (3) a new moving-target mechanic — static bodies repositioned via Body.setPosition along a sine wave, driven by a `movement: { axis, range, period }` level schema field, applied to levels 6 and 9; (4) replace the 4 geometric giblet fragment shapes with organic jittered-radius 'flesh chunk' blobs; (5) shorten/soften the rat's swing trail by activating the previously-dormant per-variant trailLength field (20/12 vs the global cap of 30) and lowering the trail's alpha multiplier
decisions.rationale: Recalibration keeps the meter/damage relationship internally consistent (pushMaxSpeed and DAMAGE_SCALE scaled by inverse factors) while raising the skill ceiling, rather than just rescaling the HUD. Moving targets reuse static bodies + Body.setPosition so collision/damage formulas need no changes — a dynamic-body approach was rejected as unnecessary complexity. Giblet blobs and trail tone-down both activate/reuse existing per-fragment and per-variant data rather than adding new state, consistent with this project's preference for repurposing dormant fields.

decisions.decision: Corrected the task-63 damage recalibration: DAMAGE_SCALE 2000→200 (a 10x cut), with damageIntensity's saturation point (24→240) and the screen-shake damage threshold (12→120, shakeIntensity divisor 8→80) scaled by the same factor to preserve their relative tuning; CLAUDE.md's HP system and Impact feedback bullets updated, and the now-disproven '~450px/60%=realistic ceiling' claim removed pending real swing-speed data.
decisions.rationale: Playtesting the tasks 63-74 round found Level 1 took 30-40 hits to clear versus the ~2-3 hits the task-63 calibration targeted — the underlying assumption (real swings reach ~60% of the new 750 pushMaxSpeed, i.e. ~450 px/step) was wrong; actual swings land far slower. DAMAGE_SCALE is the direct lever (damage is linear in 1/DAMAGE_SCALE, so hit-count scales ~linearly with it), and a straight 10x cut maps 30-40 hits to the requested ~3-4. damageIntensity and the shake threshold were tuned as a set with DAMAGE_SCALE=2000 last round, so scaling them by the same 10x keeps particle-burst and shake feel consistent with that pass's intent rather than maxing out on every routine hit. pushMaxSpeed/meter calibration is left untouched — it doesn't feed the damage formula, so it's an independent follow-up once real speed data exists.

decisions.decision: Archived all 74 completed/superseded action items to history/action-plan-archive.md, keeping only open items in project-state.json; queued a 16-item graphics/sound polish backlog (tasks 77-92) from the 2026-07-03 project review
decisions.rationale: project-state.json is re-read at every session briefing, and frameworklite’s token economy favours keeping only live items in context — the plan had grown to ~600 lines, mostly history duplicated by the decisions log. The backlog captures the review’s graphics suggestions (act theming, hit-stop/flash/decals, ribbon trail, sparks, shadow/DPR perf) and sound suggestions (master bus + compressor, jitter, whoosh, material voices, missing events, ambience), with the two big bundles gated on /brainstorm per the design gate.

decisions.decision: Game-feel bundle design (supersedes tasks 81/82/83/87/89 with tasks 93-98): inline integration (approach A) — hit-stop as a main.js timer gating the sim block (physics + gameplay timers pause, particles/shake/render continue) on the shared damage > 120 threshold, 40-80ms scaled by damageIntensity; ~2-frame white flash + velocity-aligned squash-stretch in drawRat; ground-only blood decal offscreen canvas cleared on restart; audio master GainNode -> DynamicsCompressor bus with a persisted mute toggle (no volume slider); looping whoosh tracking the 0-1 normalizedSpeed. Implementation gated behind tasks 76/45 playtests validating the current branch.
decisions.rationale: Approach A (inline, no new module) chosen for smallest blast radius over a dedicated juice.js module (abstraction ahead of need — one collision event, one consumer) and an event bus (oversized). Physics-only freeze chosen because a full render freeze reads as a dropped frame; threshold-gating avoids micro-stutter on weak hits and keeps feedback constants one tuning group. Target stains rejected (conflicts with crack overlays, removed shields, and moving targets). Mute-only chosen over a slider — the master bus makes a slider trivial later. Whoosh tracks normalized speed so it inherits rather than duplicates the unvalidated meter calibration (task 77).

decisions.decision: Merged branch swinging/feat/game-feel-bundle into main

Giblet gore-variety redesign (tasks 101-104): each shatter fragment gets a plugin.pieceType at spawn (guaranteed 1 bone shard / 1 organ / 1 gut coil, rest weighted flesh chunks with variant fur edge) with per-type geometry precomputed blobVerts-style; path-drawn per-type painters in drawFragments; fragment collision mask gains 0x0001 so giblets land on the floor (they previously collided only with each other and fell through — restitution/friction were dead values); first ground contact emits fragment-landed -> Renderer.paintSplat into the task-97 decal layer; airborne fragments shed small blood-drip particles on a precomputed cadence
decisions.rationale: Approach A (typed roster, path-drawn) chosen over B (sprite-baked offscreen canvases — higher detail ceiling at zero per-frame cost, but extra canvas-lifecycle machinery for fidelity likely imperceptible at ~20px/4s) and C (physics-shaped bodies — breaks the physics-untouched constraint and changes collision behavior for barely-visible payoff). All detail is baked at spawn (no per-frame randomness or shadowBlur, consistent with task 86); splats/drips reuse the existing decal and particle systems. The mask fix is the enabling change for landing splats and delivers most of the realism payoff by itself.

decisions.decision: Playtest bot + dev telemetry via approach B (Playwright driving a real browser): a ?dev=1-gated in-game instrumentation layer (js/dev/telemetry.js, bot.js, harness.js, dynamically imported so a normal player fetches nothing) plus a Node-side rig (dev/serve.mjs, run-batch.mjs, shots.mjs, npm run gate). The bot dispatches real PointerEvents in-page so input.js is exercised end-to-end; runs are seeded for reproducibility; one telemetry schema covers bot, gate and human runs, tagged by source. Tasks 105-110.
decisions.rationale: B chosen over A (two-lane harness with a Node/jsdom-stub batch lane, per L0108) and C (telemetry only, no bot). The user prioritised regression-gate plus tuning-data generation at batch scale. A was the recommendation on speed grounds — a stub lane runs dozens of games in seconds where a real browser costs wall-clock time — but B buys real render-path and real-input fidelity with no stub-drift risk, gets screenshots for free (closing task 104 durably), and parallel headless contexts should keep a 20-run batch practical. Playwright is a devDependency alongside vitest/jsdom, so spec.md's no-build-system constraint is untouched: the shipped game still loads as plain ES modules. Deliberately NOT part of this work: any change to gameplay constants (DAMAGE_SCALE, pushMaxSpeed, thresholds) — this measures, and tuning is a separate decision once numbers exist. Standing caveat: a bot's swing profile is not a human's, so bot data is valid for regression detection and relative A/B of constants, while absolute calibration must rest on human-run telemetry — calibrating constants on bot swings would repeat the L0097 unmeasured-premise error that produced the 30-40-hit Level 1.

decisions.decision: Playtest findings from the first instrumented session: (1) no ordinary target can be destroyed - physics.js:84 computes a SHATTER/CRACK/SURVIVE outcome per target hit, main.js:166 destructures it and never reads it, and removeTarget has one call site (the shield branch, main.js:181), so material.strength/crackThreshold/fragmentCount/fragmentSpread are dead config and only yoyoDamage is live; (2) Acts 2-3 obstacles are bypassable - a bot whose target picker explicitly filters shields out still cleared 24/24 runs across L4-L9, with the Act 2 finale (L6) clearing in 4 hits / 2.4s against Level 1s 9 hits, an inverted difficulty curve.
decisions.rationale: Recorded as measurement, not yet as a fix. The user flagged both from play; the telemetry and a shield-avoiding bot independently confirmed them. Which way to resolve the target question is a design fork (indestructible-by-design with the misleading Brittle label removed, vs. targets becoming breakable) that changes the core loop, so it goes through the design gate rather than being patched.

decisions.decision: MEASURED human swing range (standard variant), replacing the assumption that has driven every balance decision to date. Free-swing calibration: peak 1146, p90 374, p50 177. In play across 9 runs (L2-L9): per-run peak p50 310 / max 400, sustained p50 109 (range 32-139), hits to clear min 4 / p50 6 / max 12, time to clear p50 9.5s, 35% of 66 hits glancing (angleFactor < 0.55).
decisions.rationale: The premise behind the task 63-75 miscalibration was that real swings reach ~60% of pushMaxSpeed (=450 for standard). Measurement shows that is wrong in both directions depending on what is measured: sustained in-play speed is 109, only 14.5% of pushMaxSpeed, while a free swing peaks at 1146, i.e. 153% OF the supposed maximum. pushMaxSpeed=750 is therefore not a ceiling at all, yet in actual play peaks top out near 400 (53%), so the speed meter never fills past about half while playing - it is normalised against a speed only reachable when not playing. Bot comparison: bot peak speed (p50 ~320) tracks human peaks (310) closely, but bot SUSTAINED speed (p50 ~51) is less than half the human 109, and since damage scales with speed squared the bot understates human damage per typical hit by roughly 4.5x. Level-by-level the bot is not a human proxy at all - it cleared L6 in 4 hits/2.4s where the human needed 7 hits/10.6s, and needed 9 hits on L1 where the human cleared L2 in 4. Confirms bot data is usable for regression detection and peak-speed comparison, not for difficulty or absolute tuning. NOT YET MEASURED: the heavy variant (pushMaxSpeed 625) has no calibration run, and no human run exists for L1.

decisions.decision: Segmented rope design (tasks 116-121): replace the single tail Constraint with a Matter chain of ~10 collidable bodies; TRUE WRAP (the rope may coil a bumper and shorten the effective radius) with a player-initiated yank to unwind; the rat gains collision with ground and walls. Built behind ?dev=1&rope=N so the batch can A/B it at identical seeds, flag removed on merge.
decisions.rationale: Wrap must emerge from real collision solving, so a hand-rolled Verlet rope was ruled out and the approach collapsed to a Matter body chain - the remaining variable is segment count and stiffness, which the batch runner can measure rather than guess. User chose true wrap over contact-drag-only, player-initiated release over auto-recovery or retry, and full rat/world collision. A collision-category cleanup is a hard prerequisite: ground and walls never set a collisionFilter and so inherited Matter default 0x0001, the same bit the rat uses, making it impossible for rope to collide with world geometry without colliding with the rat. The yank is deliberately energy-neutral (impulse toward the pivot plus tangential damping, on a cooldown) because an accelerating yank would become the dominant strategy; that risk is checked by measurement - a yank-spam batch must show no advantage - rather than by judgement.

decisions.decision: Rope parameters set by sweep: 10 segments, per-segment mass 5% of rat mass, engine.constraintIterations 48 while a rope is attached (Matter default 2 restored for the un-roped path). Circles of radius 3.5, stiffness 1.0, zero constraint damping, frictionAir 0.0005.
decisions.rationale: Segment mass is the dominant term and the naive value was badly wrong. At 1-2% of rat mass the rope swallowed the swing entirely - peak speed collapsed from ~320 to 40 and the bot never cleared - because a near-massless chain cannot pull a body 100x heavier through Matter sequential solver. Raising constraintIterations helps (2% mass: 102 at 20 iters, 138 at 40, 161 at 60) but does not converge to usable, so a genuinely light rope is not achievable here. At 25% per segment the rope matches the no-rope baseline but totals 2.5x the rat mass and reads as a chain rather than a tail. 5% with 40-60 iterations clears 100% of runs at median peak 208-240 against a 315 baseline, i.e. a 25-30% momentum cost, which is the hindrance the rope exists to create. Frame p95 stays 16.7ms even at 60 iterations, so iteration count is not a perf constraint. Matter default 2 constraint iterations also let the 10-link chain stretch ~30% under the rat weight, lengthening the effective pendulum from 130 to 171px; at 48 iterations the span is 131.

decisions.decision: Rope vs no-rope measured across all 9 levels and both variants (108 runs, identical seeds, fixed timestep). Result: the rope makes the game EASIER, not harder - median hits to clear 5 -> 3 (-40%), time to clear 4.1s -> 2.7s (-33%) - despite cutting peak speed 337 -> 237 (-30%). DAMAGE_SCALE and every other gameplay constant left unchanged.
decisions.rationale: The mechanism is the opposite of the intent and only measurement would have found it. Rope mass acts as a flywheel: peak speed falls 30% but SUSTAINED speed rises 23% (p50 50.1 -> 61.5) and glancing hits fall 36% (35.5% -> 22.8%). Since damage scales with speed squared and with angleFactor, a steady clean swing out-damages a peaky sloppy one, so fewer hits are needed. Momentum IS hindered as the feature intended - peak is down 30% - but peak is not what governs difficulty here. No constant was retuned because the rope moves bot median hits to clear to 3, inside the 3-4 design target, where no-rope sat at 5; the honest next step is a human re-calibration (task 121), not tuning against bot numbers. SOFT-LOCK FOUND: Level 8 with rope and no yank fails 6/6 with ZERO contacts and ZERO hits - the rope tangles slack and the bot cannot build a swing at all, so it never reaches the target. With a yank every 1.2s it clears 3/3. The yank is therefore load-bearing rather than a convenience, which retrospectively validates choosing player-initiated release over auto-recovery - but the game never tells the player that clicking yanks, so discoverability is now a real gap. Rope contacts are highest on the Act 2 shield levels L4 (80) and L6 (76).

decisions.decision: Rope tunneling root-caused to unbounded hand speed, not gravity or rope parameters. Hand rate limit and physics sub-stepping added as dev-tunable knobs (?dev=1&hand=N&subs=N) with defaults unchanged; the user will choose values by feel before they become defaults.
decisions.rationale: updatePivot wrote the pointer position directly into constraint.pointA, so the hand could teleport 234px in one frame (p50 10.6, p90 107.5) and whip the rat to a 249px/step peak against 44px bumpers. Matter has no continuous collision detection, and with p50 rat speed at 65px/step more than half of all steps already exceed a bumper diameter, so this was routine rather than a rare peak. Sub-stepping alone is not a fix: contact counts never plateau (48/39/100/157/266/288/843 at 1/2/4/8/12/16/24 sub-steps) because even 24 sub-steps leaves ~35px per sub-step, and each level is also a large difficulty change. Reducing gravity was rejected as the mechanism because the player drives the pivot directly, so player-driven speed is not bounded by gravity at all - the game would become floaty without fixing the cause. Capping the hand bounds the system where the energy actually enters. Chosen as a feel decision rather than a measured one because it caps the skill ceiling: today whipping the mouse faster is always better, which is why the human free-swing calibration hit 1146 while in-play sustained sat at 109. A correction worth recording: an earlier probe comparing body velocity against position delta was tautological, since Matter defines velocity AS the position delta, so it could not have distinguished real motion from solver correction as claimed.

decisions.decision: Rope tunneling fixed with manual continuous collision detection for rope segments only (Matter.Query.ray sweep plus an 8-step binary search for the last free point), default on. The hand cap, sub-stepping and segment speed clamp remain as dev knobs but are NOT the fix and stay at their original defaults.
decisions.rationale: No parameter could fix this. Rope segments whip to 432 px/step against 44px bumpers; sub-stepping made it marginally worse (26.3% to 30.5% over-44 from 4 to 8 sub-steps) because better constraint solving stiffens the rope; a velocity clamp cannot bound displacement because the constraint solver repositions bodies directly, independent of velocity. Matter 0.19 ships no CCD and this game sits in the regime where discrete collision fails. Sweeping is contained to the rope because the rat is large and carries the damage, so the rat speed, the hand and the game feel are untouched - unlike the hand cap, which capped the skill ceiling AND still left 26% of samples tunneling. Cost is negligible because segments moving less than their own radius are skipped, which is most of them.

decisions.decision: Rope collision strengthened with a second CCD pass at link level plus segment radius 5.0. Link crossings fall from 5-7.5% to under 1% and segment penetration stays at zero.
decisions.rationale: Per-segment sweeping fixed body penetration but not the visible clipping, because the rope is a chain of circles separated by 6px gaps and the line between two segments can cut an obstacle while neither endpoint is inside it. Closing the gap geometrically was measured and is insufficient on its own: 10 segments at radius 6.5 (zero gap) reached 2.74%, and adding segments made things WORSE (14 -> 3.11%, 20 -> 4.19%) because more links mean a floppier rope that whips harder. The link pass uses the same rewind-toward-previous-position trick as the segment sweep, so it is shape-agnostic and works for circles and rectangles alike, and it skips links that were already crossing before the step since rewinding those would freeze the rope against the obstacle. Radius 5.0 measured best of 3.5/5.0/6.5 with the link pass active.

decisions.decision: Merged branch swinging/feat/segmented-rope into main (with its stacked parents swinging/feat/playtest-bot-telemetry and swinging/feat/realistic-giblets, 20 commits)

Human calibration on the rope build. Standard: free-swing p50 133.6, p90 280.4, peak 719.6. Heavy: p50 113.1, p90 227.1, peak 784.3. Heavy pushMaxSpeed raised 625 -> 785 to match its measured ceiling; standard left at 750. DAMAGE_SCALE deliberately NOT changed.
decisions.rationale: The rope costs real momentum, now measured on a human rather than the bot: against the 2026-09-06 pre-rope calibration, standard free-swing peak fell 1146 -> 719.6 (-37%), p90 374 -> 280.4 (-25%) and p50 177 -> 133.6 (-25%). That is the hindrance the rope was built for. It also fixed the speed meter almost by accident: standard now peaks at 96% of its pushMaxSpeed where it previously hit 153% and saturated, so the meter is correctly scaled for the first time. Heavy still overshot at 125%, so its value was raised to its measured 784 - safe because pushMaxSpeed is a presentation knob with exactly one use (normalising the meter and the whoosh in main.js:420) and never enters the damage formula, which keeps balance and presentation knobs orthogonal per L0120. DAMAGE_SCALE stays at 200 because the data does not yet support a change: the only rope-build in-play runs are two Level 7 clears at 7 and 8 hits, and Level 1 - the level the 3-4 hit target was actually written against - has no rope-build run at all. Changing a damage constant on two runs of the wrong level would repeat the reasoning-from-insufficient-data error this whole effort exists to prevent.

decisions.decision: Level 1 human runs close task 127. Standard median 10.5 hits, heavy median 5 - both miss the documented 3-4 hit target, standard by about 3x. Two earlier claims corrected: heavy does NOT swing slower in play, and the bot is NOT a good proxy for human difficulty.
decisions.rationale: Measured on the level the 3-4 target was actually written against. Standard: 11/17/10/6 hits, median 10.5, 7.1s, scoring the 200 floor every time, 31% glancing. Heavy: 4/5/5/5, median 5, 3.5s, score 1000, 15% glancing. CORRECTION 1 - I previously said heavy swings ~15% slower, from free-swing calibration (p50 113 vs 134). In play the two are identical (114.1 vs 114.4), so the trade-off justifying heavy 2.2x impactMultiplier does not exist where it matters; observed damage per hit is 18.3 vs 7.7, a clean 2.4x with nothing offsetting it. CORRECTION 2 - I noted last turn that the bot appeared to track human numbers. On L1 it does not: bot standard 6 vs human 10.5, bot heavy 2 vs human 5, so the bot is roughly twice as effective as the player and the earlier agreement on L4 was coincidence. The standing caveat that bot data is for regression and relative comparison, not absolute difficulty, holds. DAMAGE_SCALE still not changed: tripling damage to bring standard to target would drop heavy to ~2 hits, so the variant imbalance (task 126) has to be resolved first or any global tuning bakes it in.

decisions.decision: Merged branch swinging/fix/speed-meter-calibration into main

Task 126 resolved by design gate: the rat variants become an explicit difficulty selector with par-relative scoring. Heavy impactMultiplier 2.2 -> 1.4, DAMAGE_SCALE 200 -> 80, per-variant parHits (standard 5, heavy 3), calcPushScore gains a parHits parameter, and the picker gets Hard/Easy labels. No score tax.
decisions.rationale: The game has no cost axis at all: the rat's only resource is HP and spending HP is winning, so impactMultiplier is one-sided and any variant carrying more of it is permanently strictly better (L0250). Reading the code settled what the task description left open - main.js:247 ends the level when the rat's own HP hits 0 and calcPushScore(hitCount) is the only scored term, so targets are anvils and hits are the sole metric. Two findings redirected the fix. First, calcPushScore has a live gradient only from 1 to 6 hits and standard's measured median of 10.5 sits four hits past the end of it, so a standard player improving 17 -> 11 hits sees no score change at all; that unscorable band, not the variant gap, is the substance of task 129, and no score multiplier addresses it. Second, the hard/easy axis is already physically real and shipped: radius 22 vs 18 produces 15% vs 31% glancing hits through angleFactor, which is a shaped cost rather than a described one (L0373). So the design keeps the precision gap as the difficulty axis, closes the unjustified raw-damage gap on top of it, and pulls both variants inside the live scoring range. Par-relative scoring was chosen over the flat score multiplier sketched in the earlier options because the 500-per-hit curve is steep enough that any sane multiplier has to be re-derived every time a hit count moves; scoring each variant against its own par lets both reach 3000 by mastery, makes standard's harder par pay more for the same absolute feat, and - with parHits defaulting to 1 - leaves the existing function behaviour and all 6 scoring tests untouched. REJECTED: per-material variant affinity (a real strategic choice, but a larger new mechanic); equalising power and differentiating on feel alone (removes strategy); relabel-plus-multiplier only (3 lines, but leaves 129 unfixed on the 200 floor). ACCEPTED CONSEQUENCES: cross-variant high scores stop being directly comparable, and saved scores earned on the old scale will be beaten easily - no migration for a single-player local game. COUPLING CHECK (L0169): three feedback constants read raw damage magnitude - damageIntensity /240, shakeIntensity /80, and hitStopTimer derived from the former - so their divisors scale by the same 2.5 (to 96 and 32) to hold felt output constant and keep hit count the only variable this change introduces (L0227). Noted while checking: damageIntensity currently peaks at 0.08 of its range, so burst scaling and hit-stop are effectively dormant at today's damage values - logged as its own task rather than fixed by accident.

decisions.decision: Add a READY state between PICKER and SWINGING: the rat starts slumped on the ground with its tail stretched out beside it, and the player grabs the tail tip to begin play. The lift is done by the game's own physics - grabbing creates the pivot constraint at the pointer, and raising the hand pulls the rope taut and hauls the rat up - rather than by an animation or a snap.
decisions.rationale: The reported glitch on entering a level was diagnosed rather than assumed: the rat spawns motionless at pivot + pushStringLength (L1: pivot y 310, rat y 440) and nothing moves until the first pointermove over the canvas, at which point the pivot TELEPORTS from the level-defined position to wherever the cursor happens to be - usually still over the Launch button - and whips the rat. A tail grab fixes this by construction, because the pointer IS the grab point, so there is no jump left to make. Chosen over two alternatives: a scripted lift tween (an input-locked animation is the same class of thing that reads as glitchy, and it re-creates in code what gravity already does) and an instant snap on grab (cheapest, but it relocates the teleport to the moment of the grab rather than removing it). The physics lift also turned out to be the LEAST code: attachRope already builds the segment chain, the segment-to-segment constraints and the rat link as separate blocks, with the pivot anchor (stringConstraint, pointA -> ropeBodies[0]) as one distinct block, so deferring that single block is the whole feature and ropeBodies[0] becomes the free tail tip that serves as the grab target. TWO CONSTRAINTS BUILT IN RATHER THAN BOLTED ON: (1) the grab is now mandatory, and an untaught mandatory affordance is a hard stop - the game cannot start at all if the player does not find it - which is L0364 logged from this very project when the yank quietly became load-bearing while still untaught; hence a prompt, a pulsing tip highlight, and a hit radius sized for touch rather than for the 5px segment body. (2) the dev rigs drive beginRun() directly (gate.mjs, run-batch.mjs, ab.mjs), so beginRun auto-grabs and no rig needs special-casing. BLOCKER FOUND DURING DESIGN: the physics floor and the drawn floor do not line up - groundBody's top surface is at y 620, the canvas bottom edge, while drawGround paints its surface line at y 580. Fragments already sink 40px into the dirt and paintSplat hides it by drawing decals at the visual line regardless of where the body actually is. A rat posed on the ground would be almost entirely buried, so aligning the ground is a required part of this change, not a bonus; it also fixes the pre-existing fragment sink. Levels are unaffected because the lowest target sits around y 459. ACCEPTED CONSEQUENCE: every level now opens with hauling the rat up, so bot baselines shift and task 133's human measurement must wait until this lands, or the rebalance gets measured twice.

decisions.decision: Tail-grab pickup accepted on feel. User played the served build and confirmed the new pick-up reads better than the old immediate start.
decisions.rationale: The feature existed to fix a perceptual complaint - entering a level 'seems glitchy' - so perceptual acceptance is the real gate and green tests could never have supplied it (same standard as task 98). Mechanical verification was already in place: 74/74 vitest, 92/92 gate across five consecutive runs, and committed screenshots of READY, the grab and the lift. NOT a substitute for task 133: an impression of the rebalance is not the recorded per-variant hit counts that 126 and 129 need.

decisions.decision: Measured the rebalance on 10 human L1 runs. Par-relative scoring is validated exactly, task 129 is closed, but the difficulty-selector premise is refuted and the variant imbalance has inverted rather than resolved.
decisions.rationale: Brown Rat/standard (par 5): 2/4500, 4/3500, 3/4000, 4/3500, 4/3500 - mean 3.4 hits, median 4, range 2-4, mean score 3800. Sewer Rat/heavy (par 3): 3/3000, 3/3000, 2/3500, 4/2500, 3/3000 - mean 3.0 hits, median 3, range 2-4, mean score 3000. THREE CONCLUSIONS. (1) VALIDATED: all 10 observed scores match calcPushScore(hits, parHits) to the point, so the implementation is correct against real play. (2) 129 CLOSED: standard L1 is median 4 hits against the 3-4 target, down from 10.5, and never touches the 200 floor - lowest score 3500. (3) 126 NOT CLOSED, AND INVERTED: standard now out-scores heavy 3800 to 3000. The prediction was wrong in a direction worth recording - standard was extrapolated to 5.2 hits from median damage-per-hit of 7.7 x 2.5, but plays at 3.4, meaning real damage per hit is nearer 29 than 19. The extrapolation failed because damage-per-hit is NOT independent of hit count: the old 10.5-hit runs were padded with weak and glancing contacts that drag the median down, and when a run only needs 3 hits those weak hits never happen. Hits-to-kill cannot be projected from a median damage sample taken at a different hit count. The knock-on is that standard's par of 5 was set from that bad prediction and is 1.6 hits too generous, handing it +800 every run, while heavy's par of 3 matches its measured 3.0. Correcting standard to par 4 centres both variants on 3000 - but it also makes explicit that the two rats now play the same, so the Hard/Easy framing has no measured difficulty behind it.

decisions.decision: Standard parHits corrected 5 -> 4 to its measured L1 median. The Hard/Easy framing is NOT settled: it is deferred until one late Act 3 level is measured, because L1 is the worst place in the game to look for a difficulty gap.
decisions.rationale: Par 5 came from an extrapolation of 5.2 hits; standard plays at 3.4 with a median of 4, so the old par handed it +800 a run and inverted the very imbalance the rebalance was meant to fix. Par 4 matches the median and brings the residual advantage down from +800 to +300, which is inside the noise at n=5. Deliberately NOT over-fitted to the 3.4 mean: par 3 would swing standard to -200 instead, and with five runs the median is the more defensible read. The framing question is separate and genuinely open. The L1 measurement says the two rats are indistinguishable (3.4 vs 3.0 mean hits), but L1 is the shortest level in the game and a 2-4 hit band has nowhere to put a gap, so concluding the variants are identical from it would be overreaching. Acts 2-3 have shields, bumpers and more targets, giving longer runs in which the precision difference (31% vs 15% glancing) has room to express itself - or to be ruled out properly. Tests survived this retune untouched because they assert against RAT_VARIANTS.parHits rather than the literals (L0352), which is exactly the case that learning was written for.
